history: Tochigi's best-documented food culture rests on two things: a year-round ritual dish, shimotsukare, built from leftovers of the New Year and Setsubun (salmon head, soybeans), and kanpyo, which is credited to the Mibu domain lord Torii Tadateru's encouragement after he was transferred from Mizuguchi in Omi to Shimotsuke-Mibu. Utsunomiya gyoza is traced to soldiers of the 14th Division stationed in the city bringing back the taste of Manchurian gyoza.
character: Cooking here is preservation- and ritual-driven rather than seafood-driven. Shimotsukare is made by coarse-grating daikon and carrot on an oni-oroshi, then simmering with salted salmon head, soybeans, aburaage and sake lees in a big pot; each household has its own version. Kanpyo is made by peeling the flesh of the yugao gourd into long ribbons and drying it in midsummer sun for two days. Utsunomiya gyoza is vegetable-heavy and mainly pan-fried.

staples.name: Shimotsukare
staples.note: Hatsuuma ritual dish: oni-oroshi daikon and carrot, salted salmon head, soybeans, aburaage and sake lees, simmered slowly; recipe varies by household.

staples.name: Kanpyo
staples.note: Dried ribbons of yugao gourd; Tochigi supplies about 99% of national output (164 t in FY2022, 99.4% per the MAFF vegetable survey), mainly Shimotsuke, Oyama and Mibu.

staples.name: Kanpyo no tamagotoji
staples.note: Kanpyo simmered and bound with egg; listed by MAFF as a Tochigi local dish.

staples.name: Kanpyo no goma-zu ae
staples.note: Kanpyo dressed with sesame and vinegar; listed by MAFF as a Tochigi local dish.

staples.name: Utsunomiya gyoza
staples.note: Vegetable-forward gyoza, pan-fried as the base style with fried and boiled versions also served; origin credited to 14th Division soldiers returning from Manchuria.

staples.name: Sekihan for Hatsuuma
staples.note: Offered with shimotsukare in a straw wrapper (warazuto) at Inari shrines on Hatsuuma.

staples.name: Mimi-udon
staples.note: Named among Tochigi local dishes in a consumer guide; no technical detail was found in the sources consulted.

staples.name: Chitake soba
staples.note: Named among Tochigi local foods in a travel account; no technical detail was found in the sources consulted.

calendar.text: Hatsuuma, the first Horse day early in the year, is when shimotsukare is cooked in a large pot and offered with sekihan at Inari shrines; one source ties the dish to the Setsubun period.
Kanpyo is harvested in July and August: gourds are peeled into ribbons and dried in strong midsummer sun for about two days, so the whole annual crop is made in these weeks.
The sources consulted give no autumn-specific data for Tochigi. Because kanpyo is a dried product, kanpyo dishes such as tamagotoji and goma-zu ae are not tied to the harvest months.
Salted salmon heads left from the New Year and soybeans left from the Setsubun bean-throwing are the stock for shimotsukare; the dish is prepared in winter ahead of Hatsuuma.

A folk saying holds that eating shimotsukare at seven houses wards off illness; treat it as custom, not a claim. No GI or brand rule for Tochigi products was confirmed in the sources consulted, and Nikko yuba and strawberries did not appear in the results, so they are omitted here.

history: MAFF describes Gunma as a flour-eating prefecture where wheat is widely grown and wheat-based local dishes such as okkirikomi, suiton and tansan manju are common. A regional explanation attributes this to well-drained soil, the dry winter karakkaze wind and long winter sunshine, which suit wheat. Yaki-manju is traced to the end of the Edo period, when Harashima Ruizo of Maebashi made miso-glazed manju.
character: The logic is wheat plus miso and soy. Okkirikomi is thick noodles simmered with vegetables; yaki-manju is a skewered steamed manju brushed with sweet miso sauce and grilled. Konnyaku, from a prefecture growing nearly all of Japan's konnyaku-imo, appears in dishes such as shira-ae. The prefecture promotes all okkirikomi variants under that single name.

staples.name: Okkirikomi
staples.note: Thick noodles simmered with vegetables; the prefecture uses the name as an umbrella for its simmered flour dishes.

staples.name: Yaki-manju
staples.note: Skewered manju brushed with sweet miso sauce and grilled; MAFF traces it to the 'miso-zuke manju' of Harashima Ruizo of Maebashi, late Edo.

staples.name: Suiton

staples.name: Tansan manju

staples.name: Konnyaku-imo
staples.note: Gunma harvested 48,500 t in the 2024 report, 95.3% of national output, on 2,990 ha (92.6%); varieties are named after the three Joumo mountains.

staples.name: Konnyaku no shira-ae
staples.note: Konnyaku in a tofu dressing, the konnyaku dish MAFF lists for Gunma.

staples.name: Shimonita negi
staples.note: Thick local leek used in dishes such as a pork-and-negi croquette in the results; no cultivation or GI detail was found.

staples.name: Mizusawa udon
staples.note: Listed as a Gunma local udon in the results; no technical detail was found in the sources consulted.

calendar.text: The sources consulted give no month-level data for Gunma. Wheat, the base of its flour dishes, is the main crop behind okkirikomi, suiton and yaki-manju.
No summer-specific food data appeared in the sources consulted; konnyaku-imo is grown in the hilly north (Hokumo) area on a large, mechanised scale.
The sources give no autumn-specific data; konnyaku-imo, which is processed into konnyaku and eaten in dishes such as shira-ae, is the crop that dominates Gunma output.
The dry karakkaze wind and long winter sunshine are the climate features cited for wheat growing, and okkirikomi is the dish promoted by the prefecture as the flour-based household soup.

notes: Gunma's konnyaku-imo share is quoted differently by year and source (about 90% in MAFF framing, 95.3% in the 2024 regional report, 97% in the 2025 MAFF overview), so always cite the year. Shimonita negi GI status and Mizusawa udon details were not found in the sources consulted and should be checked before being printed as fact.

history: Saitama's food culture is a udon culture. MAFF says the cold suttate soup of Kawajima belongs to an area where wheat was widely grown as a second crop after rice. The Musashino plateau farmhouse udon survives in western Saitama and the Tama area of Tokyo. Soka senbei grew from a speciality of Soka-juku, a post station on the Nikko Kaido highway.
character: Wheat noodles carry the cuisine, served in several local forms: Fukaya's nibotou, wide fresh noodles simmered raw into a thickened soy-based soup with local vegetables including Fukaya negi, and suttate, a cold dipping soup of vegetables ground in a suribachi. Fukaya negi is the regional signature vegetable. In the north-east granary zone, iga manju is a tansan manju coated with sekihan.

staples.name: Fukaya negi
staples.note: Leek of Fukaya city, used in nibotou, miso udon and negi dishes.

staples.name: Nibotou

staples.name: Musashino udon

staples.note: Named alongside Kawahaba as local udon styles of the 'udon republic'; no technical detail was found.

staples.name: Suttate
staples.note: Kawajima cold soup of mortar-ground vegetables used as a dipping sauce for udon; MAFF lists it as hiyajiru/suttate.

staples.name: Iga manju
staples.note: Tansan manju coated with sekihan; said to originate in Konosu (former Kawasato), eaten in the north-east grain area.

staples.name: Soka senbei

staples.name: Fukaya negi and pork miso udon

staples.note: A modern Fukaya udon presentation featuring the local leek; described in a blog, not an official source.

calendar.text: The sources consulted give no month-level data for Saitama; what is documented is the wheat second crop grown after rice, which underlies the prefecture's udon dishes.
Suttate, a cold soup of mortar-ground vegetables for dipping udon, is Kawajima's signature dish; MAFF lists it with hiyajiru, but gives no month, so the season is not asserted.
No autumn-specific data appeared in the sources consulted. Soka senbei and iga manju are everyday products not tied to a stated season in the results.
Fukaya's nibotou, wide fresh noodles cooked raw in a thick soy-seasoned vegetable soup including Fukaya negi, is a hot dish; the sources consulted do not state its season.

Sayama tea, nuka-zuke and any protected-name rules for Fukaya negi did not appear with usable detail in the sources consulted, so no claims are made for them.

history: Chiba's best-documented dishes come from two worlds: the fishing coast of the Boso peninsula (namerou, sangayaki) and farm-household festival food (futomaki matsuri-zushi, peanut miso). Peanuts reached Yachimata around Meiji 29 and became its speciality by early Taisho; by 1949 they covered about 80% of Yachimata's cultivated land, according to the city.
character: The coastal logic is raw fish minced with miso and aromatics, as in namerou, and then baked or steamed as sangayaki. One account gives miso rather than soy sauce because soy spills on a boat. Inland, preserved and festival food dominates: peanuts, peanut miso, and futomaki sushi whose cross-section forms a picture. Segro iwashi (sesame-pickled sardine) and kujira no tare are listed with it by MAFF.

staples.name: Namerou
staples.note: Fresh fish chopped with miso and aromatics; said to originate with Boso fishermen on boats.

staples.name: Sangayaki
staples.note: Namerou shaped and baked or steamed, said to come from taking namerou to mountain work; the name is explained as 'mountain house' in one theory.

staples.name: Futomaki matsuri-zushi
staples.note: Thick sushi roll with a pictorial cut face; origin accounts conflict (zuiki core c.1800, or late Edo); MAFF cites Sanmu, Isumi and Kisarazu areas.

No summer data were found. Namerou is a fresh-fish dish whose seasonality follows the catch, and the sources consulted do not give a species calendar.
No autumn data were found in the sources consulted, and peanut harvest months were not stated in the results; peanut miso is the preserved product made from the crop.
The consulted sources give no winter-specific data. Peanut miso is described as a preservation food, so it serves as the household standby when other food is scarce.

history: MAFF's Tokyo page and other sources centre on Edo-mae, meaning dishes from Tokyo Bay ingredients, and on fishermen's food such as Fukagawa-meshi, which began in Fukagawa (Koto ward) as a crew meal. Daimyo travelling under the sankin-kotai system brought seeds of regional vegetables to Edo, where they were selected into the Edo Tokyo vegetables now kept as fixed varieties.
character: Tokyo food in these sources comes from the bay and the nearby farms. Fukagawa-meshi is negi and raw asari simmered in miso and poured over rice. Edo Tokyo vegetables are fixed-seed (kotei-shu) varieties handed down from the Edo period, 52 varieties as of October 2024. Daikon was grown for pickling, e.g. Nerima daikon for takuan, and bettara-zuke is a listed Edo pickle.

staples.name: Fukagawa-meshi
staples.note: Negi and raw asari simmered in miso over rice, from Fukagawa fishermen's meals; revived in 1981 by the former owner of the restaurant Fukagawa-juku.

staples.name: Edo-mae
staples.note: Cooking from Tokyo Bay catch; Fukagawa-meshi, sushi and dojo nabe are given as examples.

staples.name: Komatsuna
staples.note: Named after Komatsugawa village by the legend of shogun Yoshimune; today's market komatsuna is mostly hybrid, distinct from traditional varieties.

staples.name: Nerima daikon
staples.note: Daikon from the Nerima area since the Edo period, used for takuan.

staples.name: Kameido daikon
staples.note: Grown around Kameido Katori shrine from about 1860-64 to early Showa.

staples.name: Bettara-zuke

staples.name: Edo Tokyo vegetables

calendar.text: The sources consulted give no month-level data for Tokyo; the Edo Tokyo vegetables come in many varieties, but their individual seasons were not listed in the results.
No summer-specific data were found in the sources consulted; Izu Island kusaya is a year-round dried product, described as a speciality dating from the Edo period.
Autumn data were not stated in the sources consulted. Daikon grown for pickling, such as Nerima, feeds the pickle trade including takuan.
Bettara-zuke is the Edo pickle MAFF lists for Tokyo; the sources consulted give no sale date or season for it, and none is asserted here.

The Yoshimune komatsuna story is tradition. Tsukiji and Toyosu markets, soba and sushi history did not appear in the results, so are not covered here; consult the sushi and soy sauce categories.

history: Kanagawa spans the Miura peninsula fishing and vegetable zone, Sagami Bay, Odawara and Kamakura. Misaki was among Japan's top tuna landing ports in early Showa. Odawara already made kamaboko in the Muromachi period, with volume in the late Edo period, and its reputation spread as daimyo on sankin-kotai stayed at Odawara and Hakone. Kenchin-jiru is traced to Kenchoji in Kamakura.
character: Sea products and vegetables from the Miura peninsula and the temple cooking of Kamakura define it. The Kenchoji tradition fries vegetables in oil before simmering. Misaki fishermen cooked unsold tuna heads by hanging them in a boat chimney; MAFF's oven version bakes them 3 to 4 hours on low heat. Miura is a major daikon area, with daikon dried along the coast for takuan in winter.

staples.name: Kenchin-jiru
staples.note: Vegetables fried in oil then simmered; origin debated between Chinese 'kenchan' and Kenchoji's 'Kencho-jiru', credited to Rankei Doryu.

staples.name: Maguro no kabuto-yaki
staples.note: Misaki dish: tuna head slow-roasted, said to come from fishermen steaming unsold heads on boat chimneys.

staples.name: Odawara kamaboko
staples.note: Made since the Muromachi period; large-scale production from the late Edo period.

staples.name: Nama-shirasu don
staples.note: Raw shirasu over rice, linked to Sagami Bay and Shonan landings at Kamakura and Enoshima.

staples.name: Miura daikon
staples.note: Miura peninsula daikon growing is over 100 years old; winter-dried on the shore for takuan.

staples.name: Oyama tofu dishes
staples.note: Listed by MAFF among Kanagawa traditional foods.

staples.name: Kanko-yaki
staples.note: Tsukui (Sagamihara) dish: filling wrapped in a flour skin, baked then steamed.

staples.name: Herahera dango
staples.note: Listed by MAFF among Kanagawa traditional foods; no technical detail found.

staples.name: Warihoshi daikon harihari-zuke
staples.ja: 割り干し大根のはりはり漬け
staples.note: Split dried daikon pickled; listed by MAFF.

calendar.text: The sources consulted give no month-level data for Kanagawa; shirasu landings at Sagami Bay and Shonan are documented but without a season calendar in the results.
No summer-specific data appeared in the sources consulted. Misaki tuna and Odawara kamaboko are year-round products and the results give no seasonal limits.
Daikon from the Miura peninsula is the crop behind the winter takuan trade; autumn growing is implied by the winter drying, but the results do not state months.
Winter is when daikon for takuan is hung to dry along the Miura coast, a sight MAFF calls a seasonal feature; sources consulted give no other winter data.

markets.name: Misaki

markets.name: Odawara

markets.name: Kamakura and Enoshima
markets.note: Known for shirasu from Sagami Bay and for Kenchoji's kenchin-jiru.

notes: Kenchin-jiru is also eaten in Iwate, Oita and Ibaraki with different ingredients, so state the Kamakura version explicitly. The Kenchoji legend that the first abbot reused dropped tofu is a temple anecdote. Sanma-men, aji himono and a specific Miura daikon brand rule were not confirmed in the results.

history: Niigata's documented dishes are tied to snow country and the Sea of Japan: hegi soba of the Uonuma region, a textile-weaving area, sasa-dango from a preservation tradition, and Murakami's salmon. The Uonuma district is also the Koshihikari heartland. Niigata sake is the product of heavy snow, clear water and the Echigo toji guild, which originated there.
character: Flavour logic is mild and preserved. Hegi soba binds buckwheat with fu-nori seaweed, giving a smooth, springy noodle served in a hegi, a shallow tray of thin shaved wood. Noppe is a mildly seasoned taro-based simmered soup; the sliminess of the taro is essential. Murakami cures salmon as shiobiki and as koji-fermented iizushi. Sake is tanrei-karakuchi, made from Gohyakumangoku and snowmelt water.

staples.name: Hegi soba
staples.note: Uonuma soba bound with fu-nori seaweed, served on a hegi tray; credited to the area's weaving culture and eaten since the Edo period.

staples.name: Noppe
staples.note: Taro-based mild simmered soup for festivals and New Year; ingredients vary, in the north including salmon and ikura.

staples.name: Sasa-dango
staples.note: Yomogi dumpling with sweet bean filling wrapped in bamboo leaf; origin variously a warring-states ration or a preserved dumpling of leftover rice.

staples.name: Tochio aburaage
staples.note: Large fried tofu of Tochio, Nagaoka, about 20 cm long.

staples.name: Shiobiki salmon
staples.note: Murakami salted salmon; grilled, including skin, and served as ochazuke.

staples.name: Murakami iizushi
staples.note: Salmon and kazunoko fermented with koji, a preserved dish of Murakami.

staples.name: Uonuma Koshihikari
staples.note: Rice from the snowy Uonuma district, which is described as the core Koshihikari area.

staples.name: Niigata sake
staples.note: Tanrei-karakuchi style; 89 breweries (first nationally) in one source, over 90 in another, 85 in an older one; third in output.

staples.name: Gohyakumangoku
staples.note: Sake rice named as typical of the clean, dry Niigata style.

calendar.text: The sources consulted give no month-level data for Niigata. Noppe is a New Year and gathering dish rather than a spring one, and produce seasons were not covered.
No summer-specific data appeared in the results, and hegi soba was not tied to a season there. Uonuma is the Koshihikari area, but harvest months were not stated.
The results give no autumn data directly. Salmon is the product Murakami cures as shiobiki and iizushi, but months were not stated in the sources consulted.
Winter is the snow-country season behind kan-zukuri sake brewing in Uonuma, where breweries use cold-season brewing and groundwater, and noppe is cooked mainly at New Year.

markets.name: Murakami
markets.note: Salmon town with a shop founded about 200 years ago selling shiobiki and recipes.

markets.name: Uonuma district

markets.name: Nagaoka brewery district

notes: Brewery counts differ by source and year (85, 89, 'over 90'), so cite the date. Hegi soba is covered by the Agency for Cultural Affairs '100-year food' scheme. Koshihikari acreage, the Koshihikari rule set and Echigo cedar details were not in the results and are not stated here. MAFF's child-oriented page treats hegi soba as the product of weaving and soba culture together.

history: MAFF's Toyama page ties the cuisine to a steep profile from the Tateyama range to Toyama Bay, with Goto (east) and Gosei (west) differing in culture. Toyama Bay is called a natural fish tank for buri, shiroebi and hotaruika. The Kitamae-bune trade carried Hokkaido kombu to Toyama ports, making Toyama a heavy kombu consumer, and fresh bay fish met that kombu in kobu-jime.
character: Two supply lines meet: the fresh bay catch and Kitamae-bune kombu. Kobu-jime sandwiches fish between kombu, which absorbs surface moisture and extends shelf life in the era before refrigeration. Shiroebi is eaten as sashimi, kobu-jime, in sumashi, tempura and kara-age; hotaruika as su-miso or okizuke. Himi uses buri whole, including kama, and buri shabu is popular. Masu-zushi shops each guard pressing and rice cooking.

staples.name: Himi kan-buri
staples.note: Winter yellowtail of Himi; eaten as sashimi, shioyaki of kama and cuts, and buri shabu; Himi's buri food culture is in the 100-year food scheme.

staples.name: Buri shabu
staples.note: Thin-sliced buri swished in hot broth; popular outside the prefecture.

staples.name: Shiroebi
staples.note: Toyama Bay shrimp; sashimi, kobu-jime, sumashi, tempura or kara-age.

staples.name: Hotaruika
staples.note: Eaten raw as sashimi, boiled with su-miso, or as okizuke.

staples.name: Kobu-jime
staples.note: Fish layered between kombu; formed in the Edo period from Kitamae-bune kombu and bay fish.

staples.name: Kobu-maki
staples.note: Kombu roll; spread inland from the ports of Higashi-Iwase, Fushiki and Mizuhashi.

staples.name: Tororo kombu
staples.note: Shaved kombu sold daily in Toyama shops and kept at home.

staples.name: Masu-zushi
staples.note: Pressed masu sushi; each shop's rice cooking, seasoning and pressing method is a craft secret.

calendar.text: Hotaruika is eaten raw, boiled with su-miso or as okizuke; the sources consulted do not state its season, so the month is not asserted here.
The sources consulted give no summer-specific data for Toyama. Tororo kombu is sold daily in the prefecture's shops, so kombu use is not tied to a season.
No autumn-specific data were found. Shiroebi, served as sashimi, kobu-jime, sumashi, tempura and kara-age, has no season given in the sources consulted.
Himi's kan-buri (winter yellowtail) is the headline winter product, eaten as sashimi, grilled kama and cuts, and buri shabu; the Agency for Cultural Affairs lists Himi's buri food culture.

markets.name: Himi
markets.note: Port famous for winter buri and its whole-fish eating culture.

markets.name: Higashi-Iwase, Fushiki and Mizuhashi
markets.note: Kitamae-bune ports through which kombu entered Toyama and spread.

markets.name: Rausu link
markets.note: Kombu-producing town in Hokkaido; one account says about 70% of its population has Toyama ties.
